sections.title: How does the Lagrange error bound calculator work?
sections.html:
The Lagrange error bound calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports error bound (eₘₐₓ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the polynomial degree (n), the evaluation point (x), the polynomial's center (a) and the max of next derivative (M).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: The formula behind the Lagrange error bound calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Error bound (eₘₐₓ)=the absolute value of (max of next derivative (M)) × (the absolute value of (polynomial's center (a) − evaluation point (x)), polynomial degree (n) + 1) ÷ (polynomial degree (n) + 2)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Lagrange error bound calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the polynomial degree, the evaluation point and the polynomial's center — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Lagrange error bound calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — polynomial degree for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Lagrange error bound calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns error bound (eₘₐₓ), derived from the polynomial degree, the evaluation point and the polynomial's center. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Lagrange error bound calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the polynomial degree, the evaluation point, the polynomial's center and the max of next derivative, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Is the Lagrange error bound calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
